extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humour studies, cultural critics, and social theorists
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative criteria and theoretical standards used to judge forms, functions, and ethics of humour (e.g., positive humour, superiority theory) within historical and social contexts. Focuses on how humour is appraised for moral, political, rhetorical, and therapeutic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive humour as promoting a positive mind-set
rubrics_metrics.description: Using humour ‘to actively promote a positive mind-set’ (1998: 138–9); being positively cheerful, being humorous will help to see you through the negatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an explicitly therapeutic or self-help aim: humour is deployed to foster optimism and resilience; typical of popular writers and self-help literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive humour requires optimism
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Positive humour requires optimism’ while pessimism in humour is expressed as irony, satire, sarcasm, or put-down ethnic humour (Hageseth, 1988: 60).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes types of humour by affective stance: positive humour is tied to optimistic outlooks; other forms are labeled pessimistic or critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive humour as a lifestyle or philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Therapeutic humour is ‘not an isolated moment in time’ but is ‘a lifestyle or perhaps a philosophy of life’ (Sultanoff, 1999).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of humour includes whether it is episodic or integrated into identity/way-of-being; strong endorsement implies habitual, person-level adoption (i.e., ‘someone with a good sense of humour’ rather than occasional joking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Therapeutic/adaptive benefits of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour is said to achieve wellness, creativity, adaptability, and so on; it can aid productivity and help people cope with adversity (Fredrickson et al.; Barsoux; Morreall).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as justificatory criterion: humour is judged positively when it demonstrably enhances coping, wellbeing, creativity, or workplace productivity; guidance includes cultivating positive emotions and ‘finding positive meaning’ in adversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological positivism: duty to be positive (normative pressure)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the positivism of late capitalism, experiencing positive emotions and eliminating negative emotions becomes a duty — 'each person has the duty to become a positive person' — and failure is blamed on inward defects (Peale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates positive humour not only by benefits but by its social/political implications: whether it individualizes problems, absolves systems, or exerts oppressive pressure to 'be positive'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic’s obligation to rescue negatives from amnesia
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic must resist the power of positive thinking and 'rescue the negatives from amnesia' by taking ridicule and negative aspects of humour seriously rather than dismissing them as mere lack of a positive mind-set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides evaluators to historicize and interrogate optimism's assumptions; expect to be labeled negative for doing so; recommends examining past theories to reveal neglected dimensions of ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority (degradation) theory: laughter as disparagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Superiority/degradation theory proposes that ‘the function of laughter is to accompany and give voice to what may be called the derogatory impulse in man, his tendency to look out for and to rejoice over what is mean and undignified’ (Sully).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats laughter as ethically suspect when it arises from denigration; use this criterion to judge humour that depends on belittling others or produces schadenfreude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ridicule and social order (humour as disciplinary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato/Aristotle: laughter can be controlled or encouraged to maintain order — e.g., censorship of 'impertinences of the rank and file against those in authority'; ridicule used to discipline erroneous belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative standard considers whether humour enforces hierarchies or disciplines dissent: humour that polices behaviour or reinforces authority may be judged positively by rulers and negatively by critics concerned with freedom or justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness/taste: choose the appropriate sort of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle in Rhetoric: 'some forms befit a free man and others do not' — the free man should use irony and eschew buffoonery; one should take care to choose appropriate humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment must consider audience, social standing and decorum: humour effective for persuasion might be inappropriate for a person of 'good taste' or certain social roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour as a pragmatic rhetorical tool (persuasive use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gorgias/Aristotle: 'we ought to worst our opponent’s earnest with mockery, and his mockery with earnest' — humour can be used strategically to counter an opponent's earnestness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates humour by rhetorical effectiveness: does it persuade or disarm? Also warns of a pragmatic–aesthetic conflict where effective mockery may violate standards of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy’s depiction and audience reaction (absence of pain)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle: in comedy people are depicted as 'worse than the average' and ridiculousness may be 'defined as a mistake or deformity which produces no pain or deformity to others' — comedy permits contemplation 'in a painless manner'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as criterion to differentiate comic from tragic responses: humour that exploits harmless flaws (no real harm) is treated differently than humour that produces pain in its object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical questionability of comic laughter (malice and untruth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates/Berger: laughter often combines pleasure and pain and may take pleasure in others' ignorance; 'Is there something reprehensible about comic laughter?' — laughter can be linked to malice and untruth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply an ethical lens: judge humour by whether it rejoices in vice/ignorance or serves truth/discipline; condemn laughter that takes pleasure in harmful ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/contextual sensitivity of theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories of laughter 'express the moral, aesthetic and political themes of their times' — misogelastic views mirror contemporary attitudes and should be historicized rather than simply dismissed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating humour or theories, account for historical context and shifting standards of taste; avoid anachronistic dismissal of past theorists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour and class/hierarchy (social rank matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Platonic examples: restrictions on the young reading texts that encourage impertinent laughter; Socrates 'looked down' on mockers and treated certain social actors (e.g., slave boy) as objects — humour intersects with class and status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether humour reinforces or challenges social hierarchies, and whether it dehumanizes particular groups by denying them equal participation in jocular exchange.
